analysis.one_liner: Bars bankruptcy courts from wiping out lawsuits against wealthy company insiders and affiliates who are not themselves in bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill 23-17 on November 3, 2021, but it never received a vote by the full House before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In big bankruptcies, courts sometimes issue 'nondebtor releases' — orders that shield people and companies who are not going bankrupt, like owners and executives, from lawsuits by victims, creditors, and regulators. This bill would generally stop that: a bankruptcy judge could not wipe out or block claims against those protected parties unless each claimant agrees in writing. It would also let a court dismiss a Chapter 11 case when a company was created through a restructuring in the past 10 years that moved the valuable assets out and left the liabilities behind — the maneuver behind some high-profile corporate bankruptcy filings. The House Judiciary Committee approved it 23-17, but the full House never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: People injured by corporate wrongdoing — opioid victims, asbestos victims, consumers and workers hurt by defective products or workplace failures — would keep the right to sue the wealthy individuals and affiliated companies who profited from the bankrupt firm, instead of being forced into releases they never signed. Creditors, pension funds, and state governments would also keep their claims against protected insiders.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims and creditors with claims against insiders

how_it_helps.text: Bankruptcy courts could no longer wipe out or modify the liability of non-debtors — the officers, directors, owners, or affiliated companies tied to the bankrupt firm — through a reorganization plan or a court order.

Courts could no longer block victims from pursuing their lawsuits against those protected parties; any temporary stay would be limited to 90 days unless the claimant agrees, and appeals of such stays would go straight to the federal court of appeals instead of stalling in district court.

A court would have to dismiss a Chapter 11 case if the company was created through a restructuring within the prior 10 years that split its valuable assets from its liabilities and left the shell company holding the debts.

The bill preserves releases that a claimant expressly agrees to in a signed writing, with clear notice — so genuinely voluntary settlements remain possible, and a claimant's treatment cannot be worsened for refusing.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy owners and executives of failing companies — such as the Sackler family of Purdue Pharma — would lose the bankruptcy shield that has protected them from direct lawsuits, and would face open-ended liability. Large companies that use 'divisional mergers' to split assets from liabilities before filing would lose that maneuver and its associated restructuring costs.

drawbacks.text: Nonconsensual third-party releases are often the glue that holds global settlements together: owners and executives agree to pay billions into a fund for victims only if they are released from further suits. Banning those releases could unravel deals like the Purdue Pharma settlement, leaving some victims with the right to sue but less money up front and years more litigation.

A single holdout creditor or claimant could refuse consent and effectively block a reorganization plan that hundreds of other parties support, reducing the certainty that makes large companies willing to reorganize rather than liquidate — which can cost jobs.

The ten-year lookback that lets courts dismiss Chapter 11 cases following divisional mergers reaches far into a company's past and could apply to restructurings done for ordinary business reasons, not just liability-shedding.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core rule is a fair trade in most cases: it keeps the people who profited from a company answerable to its victims while still letting anyone who truly agrees to a release sign away their claim in writing. The real cost is that some global settlements — where everyone's claims are traded in exchange for a large payout distributed to victims — become harder or impossible to assemble, and a single holdout claimant could block a reorganization that would otherwise fund recovery for thousands. The ten-year lookback on divisional mergers is aggressive, but it targets a maneuver whose main purpose is to strand liabilities with a shell. Weighed honestly, the bill favors accountability over settlement convenience, and the people who pay the price are the wealthy individuals it was aimed at.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House Judiciary Committee in a November 2021 markup, but House leadership never brought it to the floor for a vote, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill on July 28, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which he chaired.
On November 3, 2021, the Judiciary Committee held a markup session and voted 23-17 to order the bill reported to the full House with amendments.
No further action was ever recorded: the bill was never scheduled for a vote by the full House.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy owners, executives, and affiliates of bankrupt companies keep the ability to obtain court-ordered releases from victims' lawsuits, and the restructuring industry keeps the tool that makes those releases routine. Victims' right to sue remains subject to whatever a bankruptcy judge approves.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy insiders and the restructuring industry

sides.party_line_note: The committee vote was 23-17, but the record does not publish the party breakdown of that tally; the bill's six cosponsors were all Democrats, and the Senate never acted on a version of it.

industries.industry: Wealthy owners, executives, and shareholders of bankrupt companies
industries.note: The bill's central target: it removes the ability to use a company's bankruptcy to obtain a shield from victims' lawsuits. For ordinary people, this means the people behind a failed or harmful company stay answerable in court.

industries.industry: Large corporations using divisional (Texas two-step) restructurings
industries.note: The bill lets courts dismiss Chapter 11 cases when a company was built through a recent restructuring that separated assets from liabilities. That closes the main route manufacturers and other large firms used to move lawsuits into bankruptcy. Fewer liability-shifting restructurings mean more accountability for workplace injuries, defective products, and contamination.

industries.industry: Bankruptcy law firms and restructuring advisors
industries.note: The firms that design and litigate mega-restructurings lose the most powerful tool in their toolkit. Their interest lies in complex filings; victims' interest lies in being able to sue the people actually responsible.

industries.industry: Tort victims and their legal representatives
industries.note: People injured by products, opioids, asbestos, or workplace misconduct keep a real right to sue the individuals and affiliates who profited, instead of being folded into a court-approved release. Their interest runs directly alongside the public's.
